content: Rhinosinusitis refers to the inflammation of the nasal mucosa and the paranasal sinuses. The terms sinusitis and rhinosinusitis are often used interchangeably, but rhinosinusitis is preferred because inflammation of the paranasal sinuses rarely occurs without concurrent inflammation of the nasal mucosa. The primary cause of rhinosinusitis is infectious, although it can also be associated with other medical conditions such as allergies. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, and imaging or other diagnostic studies are generally unnecessary. There are no known life-threatening causes of sinusitis that could result in death or permanent disability within 24 hours if left untreated. However, the common causes of rhinosinusitis include infectious agents such as viruses, bacteria, and fungi. Viral causes include rhinovirus, influenza virus, and parainfluenza virus. Bacterial causes include Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis, Streptococcus pyogenes, and Staphylococcus aureus (commonly associated with chronic sinusitis). Pseudomonas aeruginosa is often implicated in nosocomial sinusitis, as well as in patients with cystic fibrosis or those who are immunocompromised. Anaerobic bacteria such as Prevotella, Fusobacterium, and Peptostreptococcus are also common in chronic sinusitis. Fungal causes include species such as Aspergillus, Fusarium, and members of the Mucorales group. The diagnosis of sinusitis, as per the Infectious Diseases Society of America, is based on the presence of at least two major symptoms or one major symptom and two or more minor symptoms. The American Academy of Otolaryngology, Head, and Neck Surgery defines bacterial sinusitis based on the following clinical criteria: 1. Persistent symptoms such as nasal congestion, rhinorrhea, or cough lasting 10 or more days without improvement. 2. Severe symptoms including a temperature of ≥38.5°C for 3-4 days and purulent rhinorrhea for 3-4 days. 3. Worsening symptoms characterized by the return of symptoms after initial improvement, or the development of new or recurrent fever, increased rhinorrhea, or worsening cough.g., gas or oil refineries, leather tanning, textiles). Additionally, ask about prior upper respiratory infections, tobacco use, anatomical anomalies, acid reflux disease, and the patient’s immunologic status. During the history and physical examination, look for major signs of sinusitis, such as purulent rhinorrhea, nasal obstruction, facial pain, hyposmia or anosmia, and fever. Minor signs include headache, cough, halitosis, fatigue, otalgia, and dental pain. On physical examination, assess for purulent nasal discharge, rhinolalia, edema, periorbital erythema, and tenderness to palpation or percussion over the frontal and maxillary regions. Be vigilant for signs of orbital pain, visual disturbances, facial erythema, or meningitis, as these findings warrant urgent referral to the emergency department. Avoid the inappropriate use of antibiotics in acute sinusitis, as most cases are viral in origin. Do not order imaging studies when the diagnosis is clinically evident. Additionally, avoid unnecessary use of decongestants, antihistamines, or topical steroid sprays unless specifically indicated.
